extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students of Carnegie/autobiography and 19th-century industrial history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive statements and practical lessons from an autobiographical chapter (Carnegie's early career in telegraphy and railroads). The page is a narrative but contains several normative/advisory points about speaking, discipline, career behavior, and technical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Make yourself perfectly at home before your audience, and simply talk to them, not at them. Do not try to be somebody else; be your own self and talk, never 'orate' until you can't help it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie attributes his later self-possession before audiences to debating-club experience and states these two explicit rules as guidance for effective public speaking (be natural, converse with the audience rather than declaim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by practice and seize opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever one learns to do anything he has never to wait long for an opportunity of putting his knowledge to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Carnegie's telegraph practice (playing with the key, practicing taking messages by ear, making copies for the press). The principle: practice skills proactively so you can take advantage of openings and small tasks that lead to advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take initiative and accept responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do something beyond the sphere of his duties--something which attracts the attention of those over him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie recounts giving train orders in his superior's absence—knowing the risk ('Death or Westminster Abbey')—and notes that acting beyond formal authority, when done competently, brings recognition. Also implies readiness to accept consequences if things go wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical practice for telegraphy: take messages by ear and fill gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: It was considered an accomplishment to read by sound; Carnegie practiced taking messages by ear and to 'fill up gaps instead of interrupting the sender' when lines worked poorly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He learned this method from an operator, practiced it while sweeping the operating-room, and it led to promotions and duties (e.g., maintaining communications during outages). The guidance emphasizes skill-building, mentorship, and adapting technique to imperfect conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of knowledge and relevant reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is sure to prove useful in one way or another. It always tells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie's modest knowledge of British and European affairs helped him with 'steamer news' duties and with making himself useful; participation in the Webster Literary Society focused reading toward debate topics and clarified ideas. Recommendation: read with practical application in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career advancement through contact with senior officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The battle of life is already half won by the young man who is brought personally in contact with high officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal contact and recognition by superiors (Scott, Lombaert, Thomson) aided Carnegie's advancement. Implicit guidance: seek opportunities for visibility to influential figures and perform beyond routine tasks when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentle, proportionate discipline and leniency for first offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Light but certain punishment, when necessary, is most effective. Severe punishments are not needed and a judicious pardon, for the first offense at least, is often best of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie reflects on having been perhaps too severe in his first 'court-martial' and later developing sympathy for those he punished. The managerial principle: prefer measured penalties and consider pardons for initial mistakes to produce better long-term results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be too hard on young people for mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: I have never since believed in being too hard on a young man, even if he does commit a dreadful mistake or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on his own near-disaster (losing then recovering payroll package) and subsequent career, Carnegie counsels leniency and understanding in judging youthful errors; supervisors should remember how contingent early success can be on chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ and train suitable women as telegraph operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Our experience was that young women operators were more to be relied upon than young men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie describes actively teaching girls as pupils and placing them in charge of offices (example: his cousin Maria Hogan). The practical recommendation: recruit and train women where appropriate, as they may be dependable and well-suited to the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with prudence in hazardous conditions and guard entrusted duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious during lightning storms and keep careful custody of entrusted packages; carelessness can ruin a career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: being 'noted in the office for caution during lightning storms' after nearly being struck, and losing then recovering the payroll package (which could have ruined him). Guidance: exercise caution in dangerous conditions and be meticulous with responsibilities that affect others' livelihoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue truth and reasoned inquiry in moral/theological discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: It was only the truth that could make us free, and the truth, the whole truth, we should pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the club's debates on predestination and religion: adopt truth-seeking and reasoned debate rather than adherence to dogma. This is a normative stance about intellectual conduct—seek evidence and open discussion.
